title: Distributed inference: replicas, batching, autoscaling expensive hardware
story:
The hardware that serves a large model is expensive enough that idle capacity dominates the bill. So the question is not how fast one request can be served but how few accelerators can serve the traffic — and the answer is almost entirely about how many requests you can run at once.

The naive arrangement wastes nearly everything. One request per replica means loading the weights, doing a pass for a single caller, and leaving the arithmetic units mostly idle while memory bandwidth does the work. Batching fixes that: one pass over the weights serves many callers simultaneously, so the dominant cost is amortised across everyone in the batch. Throughput rises roughly with batch size until something else binds.

What binds is memory, and the specific reason is worth knowing because it is not obvious. Kwon and colleagues set out the problem in 2023: high throughput serving requires batching many requests at a time, but systems struggle because the key-value cache memory for each request is huge and grows and shrinks dynamically, and when managed inefficiently that memory is significantly wasted by fragmentation and redundant duplication, limiting the batch size. So the constraint on batch size is not the arithmetic — it is that each in-flight request holds a cache whose size you do not know in advance.

The waste they identify is concrete. Prior systems allocated a contiguous memory chunk sized to the request's maximum possible length, causing severe internal fragmentation when actual lengths are shorter, with the chunk remaining reserved for the request's lifetime. Reserve for the worst case on every request and most of your expensive memory is holding nothing.

Their fix is a straight borrowing from operating systems, which is why it belongs in this track: an attention algorithm inspired by classical virtual memory and paging, storing the cache in fixed-size blocks mapped to non-contiguous physical memory, so contiguous logical pages may correspond to non-contiguous physical pages and physical memory need not be reserved in advance. The result is near-zero waste with flexible sharing within and across requests — the same idea that let an operating system stop giving each process a contiguous block, applied to a machine whose memory costs a great deal more.

Two operational consequences. Batching buys throughput by making requests wait for one another, so batch size is a dial between cost per request and latency of each request, and there is no setting that is good at both. And autoscaling this hardware is slow — acquiring an accelerator and loading weights takes long enough that capacity arrives after the traffic that needed it, which means you are provisioning for a forecast rather than reacting to a measurement.

problem.name: Accelerator utilisation
problem.shape: Serving a large model requires hardware expensive enough that idle capacity, not compute time, is the dominant cost.
tell: accelerator utilisation is low while the bill is high
batch size is limited and nobody can say by what
memory runs out long before arithmetic does
scale-up completes after the traffic spike has passed
problem.move: Batch aggressively and find what actually limits the batch, which is usually per-request memory rather than arithmetic. Avoid reserving worst-case memory per request — allocate in blocks as the request grows. Treat batch size as an explicit trade between cost and latency, and provision against forecasts rather than relying on reactive scaling.
problem.invariant: One pass over the weights can serve a whole batch, so the cost per request falls with batch size — and batch size is bounded by the memory each in-flight request holds, which grows dynamically and is not known in advance.
problem.breaks: Batching raises throughput by making requests wait for each other, so the setting that minimises cost per request maximises the latency of each one. There is no value that is good at both, which makes it a policy decision about which callers you are serving rather than a tuning exercise.

cost.time: queueing delay while a batch forms, paid by every request in it
cost.space: per-request cache proportional to how much has been generated so far, which is the resource that actually caps concurrency
cost.beats: one request per replica, which leaves the arithmetic idle, and worst-case reservation, which holds expensive memory that is mostly empty

worked.problem: Why is memory rather than arithmetic usually what limits how many requests you can serve at once?
worked.reasoning:
Because each in-flight request carries its own cache whose size grows as the request proceeds and is not known when it starts, and that cache — not the arithmetic units — is what runs out.

The shape of the workload is the starting point. Serving is dominated by moving weights rather than by the arithmetic performed on them, so one pass that serves a single caller leaves most of the arithmetic idle. Batching is the fix: one pass over the weights serves many callers at once, and the dominant cost is amortised across the batch. So throughput rises with batch size, and you want the batch as large as possible.

Then the cap. The paper states it directly: high throughput serving requires batching many requests at a time, but existing systems struggle because the cache memory for each request is huge and grows and shrinks dynamically, and when managed inefficiently is significantly wasted by fragmentation and redundant duplication, limiting the batch size. So what stops you adding another request to the batch is that there is nowhere to put its cache.

The specific waste is what makes this a design problem rather than a hardware one. Prior systems allocated a contiguous chunk sized to the request's maximum possible length, causing severe internal fragmentation when actual lengths are shorter, and the chunk stayed reserved for the request's lifetime. So a request that might run long reserves as though it will, and most of that expensive memory holds nothing for most of its life.

The fix borrows from operating systems, which is why it fits this track. Store the cache in fixed-size blocks that can be mapped to non-contiguous physical memory, so contiguous logical pages correspond to non-contiguous physical ones and memory need not be reserved in advance — giving near-zero waste and flexible sharing within and across requests. It is precisely the move that let operating systems stop handing each process a contiguous region, applied where memory is far more expensive.

And the relationship to scheduling is complementary rather than competing, which the authors say explicitly: interleaving requests so more can be processed in parallel increases utilisation, while managing memory better lets more working sets fit — the two compose, and they report a two to four times speedup over the scheduling approach alone.

The operational point I would add is that batching is not free to the caller. It raises throughput by making requests wait for one another, so the batch size minimising cost per request maximises the latency of each. That is a policy decision about who you are serving rather than a number to tune — and autoscaling does not rescue you, because acquiring an accelerator and loading weights takes long enough that capacity arrives after the traffic that needed it.

problem.practice: Find what currently caps your batch size — memory, a configured limit, or a latency target — and check which. Then measure cost per request and latency per request across three batch sizes and plot them against each other; that curve is the decision, and nobody can make it for you.

beats.broke: The hardware serving a model is expensive enough that idle capacity is the dominant cost, and a request-per-replica arrangement leaves most of it idle most of the time.
beats.fix: Batch requests so one pass over the weights serves many callers at once, and manage the per-request memory so batch size is limited by real usage rather than by worst-case reservation.
beats.cost: Batching buys throughput by making requests wait for one another, so the dial trades cost per request against the latency of each — and autoscaling this hardware is slow enough that capacity arrives after the traffic that needed it.

interview.q: Why is memory rather than arithmetic usually what limits how many requests you can serve at once?
interview.trap: Assuming the accelerator runs out of compute. The cache each in-flight request holds grows dynamically and was classically reserved at worst-case size, so memory runs out first — and the fix was borrowed wholesale from virtual memory paging.
